description: Kingdom in the Rhône-Saône corridor (c. 443–1032) successively Burgundian, Frankish, and then the independent Kingdom of Arles; its strategic position on the routes between France and Italy and its control of the Alpine passes made it a contested prize eventually absorbed into the Holy Roman Empire through inheritance.

temporal.notes: Distinct from Valois Duchy of Burgundy; royal title in Provence/Arles orbit.

geographic.notes: Centroid approximate; polygon pending schematic or OHM sourcing.

lifecycle_phases.description: Second Burgundian kingdom established by Rudolph I.
Rudolph II and Conrad integrate Italy; maximum Burgundian extent.
Rudolf III rules without heirs; imperial pressure builds.
Conrad II inherits; Burgundy absorbed into Holy Roman Empire.

rise_factors.description: The Rhône-Saône corridor was one of the richest agricultural regions; Burgundian wine had commercial value from an early date.
Burgundy controlled north-south land routes between the Mediterranean and northern Europe.
The second Burgundian kingdom (888–1032) consolidated territories through careful inheritance and alliance-building.
The Kingdom of Burgundy emerged from Carolingian partitions as a wealthy intermediate kingdom controlling the Rhône-Saône corridor connecting the North Sea economies with Mediterranean Italy.
Burgundy's cities, Lyon, Arles, Besançon, sat on the main commercial axis from Marseille to Flanders, generating toll revenues and supporting urban commerce throughout the 10th–11th centuries.

decline_factors.description: Rudolf III of Burgundy died without male heirs in 1032, bequeathing the kingdom to his nephew Conrad II of the Holy Roman Empire.
Absorption into the Holy Roman Empire as the Kingdom of Arles ended Burgundy as an independent political unit.
The Rudolfian dynasty lacked the military capacity to defend against imperial pressure.
Rudolf III bequeathed the Kingdom of Burgundy to Emperor Conrad II in 1032, incorporating it into the Holy Roman Empire as the Kingdom of Arles and ending its independent royal status.

Without strong royal leadership capable of commanding the great nobles, Burgundy could not mount coordinated resistance to its absorption by stronger neighbors, France, the Empire, and eventually the Valois dukes.
